M2.lead_interest: When an AI system acts on someone's personal data, how do people make sense of what it did, and how can we measure whether they understand and trust it when engagement metrics look good either way.
M2.notes: The sense-making core matches Riley's interest and avoids a privacy reframing, but the 'still have a say' agency facet is missing and direction 2 leans on industry 'metrics next to engagement' framing; the Li paragraph is an accurate bracketed placeholder. The self-claims stay within boundaries, though calling class projects 'formal research experience' is borderline wording, softened by the explicit 'modest' and course framing.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: Some of the people writing it were using the app more than before.
unsupported_self_claims.why: Memory records only that the cluster existed and went into the appendix. It does not say Riley linked these respondents to their usage data, so this is an added finding.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: It was the most interesting part of my work that year.
unsupported_self_claims.why: Memory says the note-taking was the most interesting part of Riley's month, not their year. This is a small inflation beyond the record.

REV.lead_interest: When AI systems act on people's personal data, how people make sense of what the system did, where their explanation diverges from what it actually did, and how to measure that understanding and trust.

faculty_misdescriptions.quote: "Why am I seeing this," a UIST 2025 paper she co-authored, starts from the observation that people form theories about why a personalized system showed them something but have no way to check them.
faculty_misdescriptions.why: No UIST 2025 paper by this title appears in the faculty snapshot, so the paper and its framing look invented.

REV.notes: The statement is honest about Riley's role and limited research background, and it keeps the interest framed as understanding of AI decisions rather than privacy, though it leans toward 'measuring trust' and underplays 'still having a say'. 'I ran ... a usability test' omits that the capstone was a team of 4, and the COLM'26 co-author names and result details go beyond what the snapshot records.

M3.lead_interest: What people think is happening when a system uses their own data to decide things for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say.
M3.notes: The email accurately centers Riley's agency and understanding interest without a privacy reframing, and it describes the COLM'26 autonomy paper correctly; 'roughly one in ten' is hedged and presumably came from session. Calling the class projects an 'undergraduate HCI interview study and a usability test' under limited research experience is modest but borderline, since it does not say they were class projects.

cross_material_inconsistencies: What happened to the survey finding: REV says the theme "didn't fit a sentiment score" and "went into an appendix". M3 says "Those comments ended up folded into a single sentiment score."

Survey details: REV describes the theme only as "that sentence kept coming up in different forms". M3 adds specifics that appear nowhere in REV: "roughly one in ten people said their plan had changed and they didn't know why, or asked how the app knew they'd slept badly. A couple had turned off health-data sharing."

Stated main interest: REV centers on sense-making and measurement: "how do people make sense of what it did? Where does their explanation differ from what the system actually did... How could we measure understanding and trust carefully enough". M3 shifts toward control and agency and drops measurement: "what people think is happening when a system uses their own data to decide things for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say."
cross.revision_change_summary: REV replaces M2's metrics-heavy, skills-list, job-application framing (lift numbers, enumerated research directions, industry methods) with a personal narrative about a survey response that stayed with the applicant, the limits of their analytics tools, and what they want to learn, and it adds a specific faculty fit paragraph.
